```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", out.width = "100%", fig.width = 7, fig.height = 5)
# The article downloads its prices from Yahoo Finance while it is built. The download is
# made here first, out of sight, so the chunks below get it from the disk cache, and
# without it the code is shown without its results instead of failing the build.
online <- tryCatch(
  !is.null(golemstockindices::get_history("S&P 500", as.Date("1950-01-01"))),
  error = function(e) FALSE
)
knitr::opts_chunk$set(eval = online)
```

`r if (!online) "> The prices could not be downloaded when this page was built, so the code is shown without its results."`

The Volatility, Drawdowns and Seasonality tabs of the [golemstockindices app](https://sedzinfo-golemstockindices.share.connect.posit.cloud/) work the same way in R. An `_analysis()` function does the calculations, and its result goes to three functions:

- `_text()` sums it up in sentences, as the app does above its charts;
- `plot_` draws its chart;
- `_table()`, for drawdowns and seasonality, shows its numbers as a sortable table.

All three analyses compare the present with an index's past, so pass them the whole history. [Get started](golemstockindices.html) shows how to find indices and download their prices. This page uses the S&P 500 since 1950.

```{r history}
library(golemstockindices)
spx <- get_history("S&P 500", as.Date("1950-01-01"))
```

## Volatility

`volatility_analysis()` asks whether the volatility of the last 21 trading days, and the move of the last 2 days, are normal for the index. It compares them with the index's history and with a GARCH(1,1) model, and forecasts the next 5 trading days. All its windows count trading days, and a year is 252 of them. It needs more than a year of history.

```{r volatility}
analysis <- volatility_analysis(spx)
text <- volatility_text(analysis)
text$month$headline
writeLines(strwrap(paste("-", text$month$points), width = 70, exdent = 2))
```

`volatility_text()` has two more parts, `$recent` for the last 2 days and `$forecast` for the next 5. Each has a `headline` and `points`, a character vector of sentences. The numbers behind the sentences are in the analysis, such as the forecast ranges of the next closes:

```{r forecast}
analysis$forecast$days
```

`plot_volatility()` draws three panels:

- the volatility of every 21-day period of the history, with its median and 95th percentile;
- each of the last 63 days, as its move in the standard deviations the GARCH model expected;
- the last 21 closes, followed by the forecast.

```{r plot-volatility, fig.height = 7}
plot_volatility(analysis)
```

`plot_forecast()` draws the lower panel on its own: the last 30 closes, then the median close of the next 5 trading days, with the ranges of the middle half and of 95% around it. The ranges start from the last close. Hover over the median line for the ranges of a day:

```{r plot-forecast}
plot_forecast(analysis)
```

The GARCH model needs at least 500 days before the last days. Without one, `plot_volatility()` draws only its upper panel, and `plot_forecast()` stops with an error that says there is no forecast.

The arguments of `volatility_analysis()` change the periods. For example, `month_days = 5` and `recent_days = 1` ask about the last week and the last day:

```{r volatility-week}
week <- volatility_analysis(spx, month_days = 5, recent_days = 1)
volatility_text(week)$month$headline
volatility_text(week)$recent$headline
```

`plot_volatility()` takes `days` for the days of the middle panel and `context_days` for the closes before the forecast, which `plot_forecast()` takes too. The length and the probability of the forecast are set in `volatility_analysis()`, with `forecast_days` and `level`. For example, the next 10 trading days with 90% ranges, after the last 60 closes:

```{r forecast-options}
ten_days <- volatility_analysis(spx, forecast_days = 10, level = 0.9)
plot_forecast(ten_days, context_days = 60)
```

## Drawdowns

`drawdown_analysis()` measures how far the index is below its all-time high, and lists its earlier falls of 20% or more with how long they took to recover:

```{r drawdowns}
falls <- drawdown_analysis(spx)
now <- drawdown_text(falls)$now
now$headline
writeLines(strwrap(paste("-", now$points), width = 70, exdent = 2))
```

The falls are in `falls$episodes`, the deepest first. A fall that has not got back to its high yet is marked `ongoing`:

```{r episodes}
columns <- c("peak_date", "trough_date", "depth_pct",
             "recovery_date", "days_total", "ongoing")
head(falls$episodes[, columns])
```

`plot_drawdowns()` draws the close on a log scale with the all-time high so far, and under it the drawdown. The falls are shaded from their peak to their recovery, the current one in amber, and their troughs are numbered by depth:

```{r plot-drawdowns, fig.height = 6}
plot_drawdowns(falls)
```

`drawdown_table()` shows the same falls as a sortable table:

::: {style="overflow-x: auto;"}
```{r drawdown-table}
drawdown_table(falls)
```
:::

To list smaller falls as well, lower `min_depth`, for example `drawdown_analysis(spx, min_depth = 10)`.

## Seasonality

`seasonality_analysis()` asks whether some periods bring better returns than others. The period is one of:

- `"day"`, the days of the week;
- `"week"`, the weeks of the year;
- `"month"`, the months;
- `"year"`, the years of the US presidential cycle.

A Kruskal-Wallis test then asks whether the differences could be chance.

```{r seasonality}
months <- seasonality_analysis(spx, "month")
text <- seasonality_text(months)
text$groups$headline
text$chance$headline
```

The `$points` of each part give the details, such as the p-value of the test and how many months it compared.

`plot_seasonality()` shows the mean return of each group, with the median as a diamond, and under it the share of returns above 0. Hover over a bar for all the numbers of its group:

```{r plot-seasonality}
plot_seasonality(months)
```

`seasonality_table()` shows the numbers as a table:

::: {style="overflow-x: auto;"}
```{r seasonality-table}
seasonality_table(months)
```
:::

The other periods work the same way, for example the days of the week:

```{r seasonality-day}
plot_seasonality(seasonality_analysis(spx, "day"))
```

## Dark mode and saving

Like the price charts, every `plot_` function takes `mode = "dark"` for a dark page. The charts are plotly objects, and the tables are DT tables, so `htmlwidgets::saveWidget()` saves any of them as a web page:

```{r save, eval = FALSE}
htmlwidgets::saveWidget(plot_drawdowns(falls), "drawdowns.html")
htmlwidgets::saveWidget(drawdown_table(falls), "drawdowns_table.html")
```
